answer:
I built a random circuit on 8 connected Garnet qubits (QB1, QB2, QB4, QB5, QB3, QB9, QB8, QB10, chosen so every two-qubit gate sits on a real Garnet coupler). It has 10 layers. Each layer applies random single-qubit gates, then CZ gates on a random set of non-overlapping couplers. That is 35 CZ gates in total, and 10 layers satisfies the at-least-8 requirement. I ran it once with 1000 shots on garnet:mock (job 01a16041-c619-7072-ae62-7f23f41262f5). No real QPU credits were spent. I computed the ideal output probabilities on my laptop and scored the samples with linear XEB.

Results: xeb_ideal = 0.975 and xeb_measured = 0.255. xeb_ideal is the score a perfect quantum computer would get. It is close to 1 because a random circuit does not spread probability evenly. Some bitstrings are much more likely than others, and a perfect sampler lands on those. xeb_measured is the score the returned samples actually got. Its distance from 0.975 is the noise.

What the score means: XEB is 2^n times the average ideal probability of the bitstrings you measured, minus 1. A score near 1 means the device samples like the ideal circuit. A score near 0 means the samples look like uniform random noise. A score between the two means a partly faithful run. On a real chip the score falls roughly exponentially with the number of gates, because each gate adds a little error. A score clearly above 0 is evidence that the hardware really ran the circuit. Google's advantage claim rests on this: it showed a small but clearly nonzero XEB at 53 qubits, where checking by classical computer takes huge effort.

Important caveat: this was the mock device, not real hardware. The mock is a noisy emulator. It returned only 8 distinct bitstrings out of 256 possible, so its output is not a faithful picture of an ideal run. The 0.255 therefore shows how to compute the benchmark. It is not a measurement of real Garnet quality. A real Garnet run would cost credits, and I did not do one because it was not requested.

Why 8 qubits is easy for a laptop and 50 or more is not: an n-qubit state needs 2^n complex numbers. For 8 qubits that is 256 numbers, which is tiny. My laptop simulated the whole circuit instantly. At 30 qubits it is about a billion numbers. At 50 qubits it is about 10^15 numbers, which is petabytes of memory. At 53 qubits, the size used in the advantage experiments, it is about 9 quadrillion. Each added qubit doubles the memory and the work. XEB also needs the ideal probabilities from that classical simulation, so checking a large device is itself very hard for classical machines. The quantum computer does this with only n physical qubits, which is why random circuit sampling is the task where it is claimed to win. Note that the task is chosen to be hard for classical machines and has no known practical use.
